notable_claims: Personal non-commercial computer use should be tolerated if it does not substantially increase costs.
Universities should grant a right to email privacy, and Congress should eventually codify this legally.
The risk of university liability for user postings on email or Usenet is hypothetical and should be tolerated.
Electronic publication via mailing lists and Usenet extends freedom of the press beyond print media.
classification.summary: John McCarthy outlines proposed policies for university computer use, advocating for the tolerance of personal non-commercial use. He argues for a guaranteed right to email privacy and suggests that universities should not fear liability for user content on email or Usenet. Additionally, he posits that computers extend freedom of the press by lowering the cost of electronic publication.
classification.title: Computers and Academic Freedom mailing list (batch edition)

identity.subject: Computers and Academic Freedom mailing list (batch edition)

notable_claims: NCSA policy granted the director the right to monitor email
Warning users that mail may be opened is insufficient justification for doing so
classification.summary: The author critiques a National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) policy that grants the director the right to monitor email. The post notes that while NCSA requested suggestions for revising the policy from a university committee, the monitoring authority remained in place. The author argues that providing a warning about potential mail interception does not justify the act of opening it.
classification.title: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom

identity.subject: Re: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom

notable_claims: Users own the information in their disk files even if they do not own the physical disk.
Email and newsgroup access are essential components of freedom of expression.
Computer and network access should not be denied without due process.
Resource limitations should be managed via quotas rather than restrictions on how resources are used.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie proposes a framework for academic freedoms as applied to computers. He categorizes these rights into freedom of expression, privacy, due process, access, and resource limits. The proposal emphasizes that users own the information in their files regardless of hardware ownership.
classification.title: Which rights?

notable_claims: Information in a user's disk files is private regardless of who owns the hardware.
University members retain constitutional privacy rights that extend to assigned offices and residence halls.
Search warrants should be required prior to searching electronic or physical academic spaces.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that privacy rights for electronic files should be analogous to the privacy of physical desks and offices. He cites university student codes and ACLU guidance on Fourth Amendment rights to argue against the notion that working at a public university eliminates an individual's right to privacy.
classification.title: RE: Which rights?

notable_claims: Institutions use account registration forms to force users to waive privacy rights regarding file searches.
Students should have clearly defined means to participate in the formulation of institutional policy affecting academic affairs.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the necessity of an appeals process for institutional rules and argues that students and faculty should participate in policy formulation. He specifically criticizes the practice of requiring users to sign waivers granting institutions unrestricted access to their files as a condition for obtaining computer accounts.
classification.title: Which Rights?

notable_claims: Newsgroups are functionally equivalent to serials/periodicals.
Electronic journals on Usenet have been assigned ISSN numbers.
The American Library Association's Freedom To Read statement applies to electronic newsgroups if they are treated as library materials.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie argues that Usenet newsgroups should be classified as serials or periodicals rather than mere communication tools. He contends that this classification brings them under the protection of existing library policies, such as the American Library Association's Freedom To Read statement. The post provides evidence of electronic journals receiving ISSN numbers and professional recognition from Library Journal.
classification.title: Re: Which Rights?

notable_claims: The archive contains a wide array of university computing ethics and policy statements from institutions such as Baylor, Columbia, and Purdue.
Professor John McCarthy led an effort to restore the 'rec.humor.funny' newsgroup at Stanford University after it was suppressed in 1989.
The NCSA revised its email policy on April 23, 1991, shortly after a critique claimed the policy was inconsistent with the Constitution and academic freedom.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie announces the availability of the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) archive via anonymous FTP at eff.org. The archive includes back issues of CAF-news, a collection of university computer policy statements sourced from the Computer Underground Digest, and documents regarding email privacy and censorship.
classification.title: New to the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) archive

identity.subject: New to the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) archive

notable_claims: University computing policies are often heavy on prohibitions and light on permissions.
Institutional policy typically evolves from informal to proscriptive, then to a balance of rights and responsibilities.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie argues that university computing policies typically evolve from no policy to overly proscriptive regulations, and finally to a balance of rights and responsibilities. To illustrate this pattern, he provides a detailed historical case study of student policy evolution at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign from 1904 to 1973. He suggests that understanding this general institutional trajectory can help guide the development of academic computer policy.
classification.title: From Regulations to Rights: The Maturation of Policy

identity.subject: From Regulations to Rights: The Maturation of Policy

notable_claims: The BU IT policy allows the university to inspect any data or file without notice.
The policy prohibits making 'offensive or annoying material' accessible.
The policy allows for amendments at any time without prior notice.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the Boston University Information Technology ethics policy from March 1990. He argues that the policy's terms regarding data inspection and 'offensive material' violate privacy and speech rights if applied to the broader campus. The critique highlights the tension between institutional IT policies and academic freedom.
classification.title: Re: Harrassment via email

notable_claims: The OCF is dedicated to obtaining and managing open computing resources so no member of the campus community is denied resources they seek.
No small number of people should control the accessibility of OCF sponsored computing facilities.
All official OCF documents must be provided to interested parties without undue delay.
classification.summary: This item provides the full text of the Constitution for the Open Computing Facility (OCF) at UC Berkeley. The document outlines a democratic governance structure designed to ensure open access to computing resources and prevent control by a small group of people. It includes a Bill of Rights covering nondiscrimination, privacy, and freedom of information.
classification.title: The OCF Constitution

identity.subject: Re: Need info on computer acct policy

notable_claims: System administrators are not responsible for correcting irresponsible user behavior regarding disk space.
Institutional resource conflicts can be resolved via departmental billing or increasing hardware capacity.
classification.summary: Joe Buck responds to Sanjay Kapur regarding the tension between system administration and user behavior concerning disk quotas. Buck argues that administrators should not intervene in irresponsible user habits, as users will eventually be forced to manage their own space. He suggests that institutional resource shortages should be solved through departmental billing or purchasing more hardware.
classification.title: Re: Email privacy vs. System management

identity.subject: Re: Email privacy vs. System management
